Theme

Time, the calendar & feasts

long ago adverb

also a long time ago, long since, not so long ago, not long ago, some time ago, a while ago, sometime ago

classical

Cic. Rosc. Com. 42: is jam prīdem mortuus est (Lewis & Short s.v. jamprīdem)
Traupman 86

jam prīdem

long ago, long since

With a past tense it says that something happened long ago; with a present, that it has been so for a long time (see already). “Ago” with a number is abhinc: abhinc decem annōs.

Other words

  • haud ita prīdem (nōn ita prīdem) — not so long ago

    also used · classical · Hor. S. 2.2.46: haud ita prīdem (Lewis & Short s.v. prīdem); Cic. Brut. 41: nostrā cīvitāte nōn ita prīdem dominātū rēgiō līberātā (Lewis & Short); Traupman 86

  • prīdem — some time ago, long ago

    also used · classical · Traupman 86, 89 · Wiktionary

  • dūdum — a while ago, just now, earlier

    also used · classical · Plaut. Amph. 2.2.59: Dūdum? Quam dūdum istuc factum est? (Lewis & Short); Traupman 86, 89, 394, 395 · Wiktionary

    (vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.; Cic. in epistulīs)

    A shorter time than prīdem: earlier today, a little while ago. Lewis & Short note that outside comedy, Cicero's letters and philosophical works and Vergil it is rare except in jam dūdum.

  • jamdūdum — long since, a long time ago; for a long time now

    also used · classical · Ter. Eun. 738: ego jamdūdum hīc adsum (Lewis & Short); Traupman 270 · Wiktionary

    Often “for a good while now”, of something still going on.

See also ago, how long ago?, a little while ago, already, once upon a time.

SourcesLewis & Short: jampridem · Lewis & Short: pridem · Lewis & Short: dudum
